---
title: "Time series and trends"
description: "Lines, areas, streams, calendars, Gantt charts and candlesticks."
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ddplot)
library(ggplot2) # economics
```

Charts for data indexed by time. `line_chart()` is the workhorse: it handles several series, `ts` objects, zooming, annotations and forecast ribbons. The others cover totals and their components, ranges, many categories at once, and daily patterns.

::: {.dd-chooser}

| Chart | Use it when |
|---|---|
| [`line_chart()`](#line_chart) | You track one or many series over time and want to zoom, compare and annotate |
| [`area_chart()`](#area_chart) | The volume under the line matters, or you show a series above and below a baseline |
| [`stacked_area_chart()`](#stacked_area_chart) | You show a total and how each component contributes over time, in values or shares |
| [`area_band()`](#area_band) | You show a range over time, such as a min/max or an interval, with or without a central line |
| [`streamgraph()`](#streamgraph) | Many categories change over time and the overall shape matters more than exact values |
| [`calendar_heatmap()`](#calendar_heatmap) | You look for daily, weekly or seasonal patterns in a daily series |
| [`anim_line_chart()`](#anim_line_chart) | You present a single series and want it to draw itself on click |
| [`gantt_chart()`](#gantt_chart) | You plan or report tasks over time, with groups, progress, dependencies and milestones |
| [`candlestick_chart()`](#candlestick_chart) | You show the open, high, low and close prices of each period, with volumes and moving averages |

:::

## `line_chart()` {#line_chart}

`line_chart()` is built for time series. It draws one or many series and comes with the interactions people expect from financial and monitoring dashboards:

- a **crosshair tooltip** that shows every series at the hovered date, sorted by value, with the series nearest to the pointer highlighted;
- an **interactive legend**: click to hide or show a series, double-click to isolate it;
- **direct labels** at the end of each line;
- **zooming**: range buttons (1M, 6M, YTD, 1Y, 5Y, All, chosen from the data's frequency), a **navigator** with a brush under the chart, and drag on the chart to zoom into a range (double-click to reset). The y axis rescales to the data in view.

A `ts` object can be passed directly. Monthly, quarterly and yearly series get exact calendar dates; for other frequencies the dates are interpolated from the time index, so use a data frame with a real date column when exact dates matter:

```{r}
line_chart(AirPassengers, y = "passengers", title = "Airline passengers, 1949-1960")
```

The data frame interface needs a date column (`Date`, `POSIXct`, "yyyy-mm-dd" strings, or numbers such as years) and one or several value columns:

```{r}
airpassengers <- data.frame(
  passengers = as.matrix(AirPassengers),
  date = zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers))
)

line_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  curve = "curveMonotoneX",
  area = TRUE
)
```

### Several series and rebasing

Pass several `y` columns (wide data), a `group` column (long data), or an `mts` object. With `transform = "index"`, every series is rebased to 100 at the first visible date. Zoom with the range buttons or the navigator and the comparison is recomputed from the new starting point; `transform = "percent"` shows the change since that point instead.

```{r}
line_chart(
  EuStockMarkets,
  transform = "index",
  title = "European stock indices",
  subtitle = "Daily closing prices, rebased to 100 at the start of the visible range"
)
```

```{r}
library(gapminder)

countries <- gapminder[gapminder$country %in% c("China", "India", "United States",
                                                "Brazil", "Nigeria", "Germany"), ]

line_chart(
  countries,
  x = "year",
  y = "lifeExp",
  group = "country",
  points = TRUE,
  curve = "curveMonotoneX",
  title = "Life expectancy at birth",
  y_title = "Years"
)
```

### Annotations: periods, events and reference lines

`bands` shades periods (here the NBER recessions), `events` marks dates with a vertical line, and `h_lines` draws reference values.

```{r}
recessions <- data.frame(
  start = as.Date(c("1969-12-01", "1973-11-01", "1980-01-01", "1981-07-01",
                    "1990-07-01", "2001-03-01", "2007-12-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("1970-11-01", "1975-03-01", "1980-07-01", "1982-11-01",
                    "1991-03-01", "2001-11-01", "2009-06-01"))
)

line_chart(
  economics,
  x = "date",
  y = "unemploy",
  area = TRUE,
  bands = recessions,
  value_format = ",.0f",
  value_suffix = "k",
  title = "US unemployment",
  subtitle = "Thousands of persons, recessions shaded"
)
```

### Forecasts and moving averages

`lower` and `upper` draw a confidence or forecast ribbon around a line. Here a Holt-Winters forecast from base R's `stats` package:

```{r}
fit <- HoltWinters(log(AirPassengers))
fc <- predict(fit, n.ahead = 24, prediction.interval = TRUE)

passengers <- rbind(
  data.frame(date = zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers)),
             value = as.numeric(AirPassengers), lo = NA, hi = NA,
             series = "Observed"),
  data.frame(date = zoo::as.Date(time(fc)), value = exp(fc[, "fit"]),
             lo = exp(fc[, "lwr"]), hi = exp(fc[, "upr"]),
             series = "Forecast")
)

line_chart(
  passengers,
  x = "date", y = "value", group = "series",
  lower = "lo", upper = "hi",
  colors = c(Observed = "#4269d0", Forecast = "#ff725c"),
  events = c("Forecast starts" = as.Date("1961-01-01")),
  value_format = ",.0f",
  title = "Airline passengers: Holt-Winters forecast"
)
```

`roll_mean` draws a trailing moving average over the raw series, which is kept as a faint line (`show_raw = FALSE` hides it). Missing values leave gaps in the lines:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
samples <- data.frame(
  time = seq(as.POSIXct("2026-03-01 09:00", tz = "UTC"), by = "5 min", length.out = 400),
  cpu  = 40 + cumsum(rnorm(400)),
  mem  = 60 + cumsum(rnorm(400, 0, 0.5))
)
samples$cpu[150:170] <- NA # a monitoring outage

line_chart(
  samples,
  x = "time",
  y = c("cpu", "mem"),
  roll_mean = 12,
  h_lines = c(SLA = 70),
  value_suffix = "%",
  title = "Server load",
  subtitle = "5-minute samples with a 1-hour moving average"
)
```

Other options include `y_scale = "log"`, `y_zero`, `date_format`, and turning off `navigator`, `range_buttons`, `zoom`, `legend`, `end_labels` or `animate`.

## `area_chart()` {#area_chart}

`area_chart()` fills the area under the line, which suits volumes and totals. It shares the interactions of `line_chart()`: crosshair tooltip, range buttons, navigator, drag-to-zoom (double-click to reset), and a clickable legend with several series. A `ts` object can be passed directly, and the classic data frame interface still works:

```{r}
area_chart(AirPassengers, y = "passengers", title = "Airline passengers")
```

With `baseline`, the area is drawn between the line and that value instead of zero, and `negative_fill` colours the part below it. This is the usual way to show anomalies, balances or a value against its average:

```{r}
area_chart(
  economics,
  x = "date",
  y = "psavert",
  baseline = mean(economics$psavert),
  fill = "#3ca951",
  negative_fill = "#ff725c",
  value_suffix = "%",
  title = "US personal savings rate",
  subtitle = "Above and below its long-run average"
)
```

The area is filled with a gradient by default; `opacity` gives a flat fill instead, `stroke` and `stroke_width` style the line on top. Several series (`y = c(...)`, `group` or an `mts` object) are drawn on top of each other; to add them up, use `stacked_area_chart()`.

## `stacked_area_chart()` {#stacked_area_chart}

`stacked_area_chart()` stacks several series so you can read both the total and how each component contributes to it. The buttons at the top right switch between stacked values and shares of the total (100%). Hover the chart to read every layer with its share and the total; click a legend entry to hide a layer (the others re-stack), double-click it to keep only that layer.

The data can be wide, as in this example adapted from [Mike Bostock's stacked area chart](https://observablehq.com/@d3/stacked-area-chart): every numeric column other than `x` becomes a layer (or the columns named in `y`).

```{r}
data <- data.frame(
  date = c(
    "2000-01-01", "2000-02-01", "2000-03-01", "2000-04-01",
    "2000-05-01", "2000-06-01", "2000-07-01",
    "2000-08-01", "2000-09-01", "2000-10-01"
  ),
  Trade = c(
    2000,1023, 983, 2793, 1821, 1837, 1792, 1853, 791, 739
  ),
  Manufacturing = c(
    734, 694, 739, 736, 685, 621, 708, 685, 667, 693
  ),
  Leisure = c(
    1782, 1779, 1789, 658, 675, 833, 786, 675, 636, 691
  ),
  Agriculture = c(
    655, 587,623, 517, 561, 2545, 636, 584, 559, 2504
  )
)

stacked_area_chart(
  data = data,
  x = "date",
  curve = "curveMonotoneX",
  stroke = "white",
  title = "Employment by sector"
)
```

`curve = "curveMonotoneX"` gives smooth layers that never cross; curves such as `"curveCardinal"` can overshoot and make layers overlap. `stroke = "white"` draws a thin separator between the layers.

Long data works too, with one value column and a `group` column. Here the chart starts in the 100% layout (`position = "percent"`):

```{r}
stacked_area_chart(
  subset(economics_long, variable %in% c("pce", "psavert", "uempmed")),
  x = "date",
  y = "value",
  group = "variable",
  position = "percent",
  title = "Composition over time"
)
```

The colours come from the ddplot palette; `colors` sets them yourself, and `color_category` picks a [D3 categorical scheme](https://github.com/d3/d3-scale-chromatic#categorical) such as `"Tableau10"` or `"Set2"`. Missing values count as zero when stacking, and negative values are stacked below zero.

## `area_band()` {#area_band}

`area_band()` shades the range between a lower and an upper value over time: a daily minimum and maximum, a confidence interval, a target range. Hover it to read the range at each date.

```{r}
airpassengers <- data.frame(
  passengers_lower = as.matrix(AirPassengers),
  passengers_upper = as.matrix(AirPassengers) + 40,
  date = zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers))
)

area_band(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y_lower = "passengers_lower",
  y_upper = "passengers_upper",
  fill = "#efb118",
  stroke = "#9c6b4e"
)
```

`y` adds a line inside the band (a mean or a median, for example) and `group` draws one band per group, with a clickable legend. `fill` colours the band and its line; `stroke` outlines the band.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
days <- seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), by = "day", length.out = 120)
temps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Oslo", "Madrid"), function(city) {
  base <- if (city == "Oslo") -2 else 9
  mid <- base + 8 * sin(seq_along(days) / 38) + rnorm(120, 0, 1)
  data.frame(date = days, city = city, mean = mid,
             low = mid - runif(120, 2, 5), high = mid + runif(120, 2, 5))
}))

area_band(
  temps,
  x = "date",
  y_lower = "low",
  y_upper = "high",
  y = "mean",
  group = "city",
  value_format = ".1f",
  value_suffix = " °C",
  title = "Daily temperatures",
  subtitle = "Mean, with the daily minimum and maximum"
)
```

## `streamgraph()` {#streamgraph}

`streamgraph()` is inspired by the [Highcharts](https://www.highcharts.com/) streamgraph: stacked areas flowing around a centred (wiggle) baseline, with labels drawn inside each layer, a crosshair tooltip and an interactive legend. Unlike `stacked_area_chart()`, it takes long data. Hover over a layer to highlight it, and click a legend item to hide or show it.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
years  <- 1980:2020
genres <- c("Rock", "Pop", "Hip hop", "Electronic", "Country",
            "R&B", "Jazz", "Metal", "Reggae", "Latin")
peaks  <- c(1984, 1999, 2012, 2008, 1993, 2003, 1981, 1990, 1986, 2018)
sizes  <- c(60, 55, 70, 40, 30, 35, 18, 25, 15, 45)
music  <- expand.grid(year = years, genre = genres)
idx    <- match(music$genre, genres)
music$listeners <- round(
  sizes[idx] * exp(-((music$year - peaks[idx]) / 9)^2) + runif(nrow(music), 1, 6)
)

streamgraph(
  data        = music,
  x           = "year",
  group       = "genre",
  value       = "listeners",
  value_format = ",.0f",
  x_title      = "Year",
  title       = "Music genres, 1980-2020 (simulated listeners)"
)
```

`offset = "expand"` turns the stream into a 100% stacked view:

```{r}
phones <- data.frame(
  year   = rep(as.numeric(rownames(WorldPhones)), ncol(WorldPhones)),
  region = factor(rep(colnames(WorldPhones), each = nrow(WorldPhones)),
                  levels = colnames(WorldPhones)),
  phones = as.vector(WorldPhones)
)

streamgraph(phones, x = "year", group = "region", value = "phones",
            offset = "expand", order = "descending", curve = "monotoneX",
            color_palette = "Set2", title = "Share of telephones by region")
```

## `calendar_heatmap()` {#calendar_heatmap}

`calendar_heatmap()` is inspired by the signature heatmap of [Frappe Charts](https://frappe.io/charts) and by GitHub's contribution graph. It draws one rounded square per day on a week-by-weekday grid, one panel per year, with a "Less ... More" legend and a staggered fade-in. Hover over a day to see its value, or over a legend square to highlight every day in that color bucket.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
days <- seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), as.Date("2026-12-31"), by = "day")
weekday <- !(format(days, "%u") %in% c("6", "7"))
activity <- data.frame(
  day     = days,
  commits = rpois(length(days), ifelse(weekday, 6, 1.5)) * rbinom(length(days), 1, 0.8)
)

calendar_heatmap(activity, date = "day", value = "commits", title = "Commits in 2026")
```

Data spanning several years is drawn as one panel per year:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
days <- seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "day")
season <- 10 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * as.numeric(format(days, "%j")) / 365)
rainfall <- data.frame(day = days, rain = pmax(0, rnorm(length(days), season, 6)))

calendar_heatmap(
  rainfall, date = "day", value = "rain", week_start = "monday",
  colors = c("#9be9a8", "#40c463", "#30a14e", "#216e39"),
  value_label = "mm of rain", value_format = ",.1f",
  title = "Daily rainfall, 2021-2023"
)
```

## `anim_line_chart()` {#anim_line_chart}

Heavily inspired by [Jure Stabuc's example](https://observablehq.com/@jurestabuc/animated-line-chart), `anim_line_chart()` draws an empty frame, and each click on it plays an animation that draws the line. The line stays in place once the animation ends. Click on the empty chart below:

```{r}
passengers_df <- data.frame(
  passengers = as.matrix(AirPassengers),
  date = zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers))
)

anim_line_chart(
  data = passengers_df,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  duration = 10000, # in milliseconds (10 seconds)
  curve = "curveCardinal"
  )
```

## `gantt_chart()` {#gantt_chart}

A Gantt chart draws tasks as bars from their start to their end. Tasks can be coloured by `group`, show how far along they are (`progress`, between 0 and 1), depend on other tasks (`depends_on`, drawn as arrows), and be compared with `today`. A task that starts and ends on the same date is a milestone. Hover a task to highlight the tasks it depends on and the ones that depend on it; scroll to zoom in time and double-click to reset.

```{r}
plan <- data.frame(
  task = c("Kick-off", "Research", "Design", "Prototype", "User tests",
           "Build", "QA", "Launch"),
  start = as.Date(c("2025-01-06", "2025-01-07", "2025-01-27", "2025-02-17",
                    "2025-03-10", "2025-03-03", "2025-04-14", "2025-05-05")),
  end = as.Date(c("2025-01-06", "2025-01-31", "2025-02-21", "2025-03-07",
                  "2025-03-21", "2025-04-18", "2025-05-02", "2025-05-05")),
  team = c("All", "Design", "Design", "Engineering", "Design",
           "Engineering", "Engineering", "All"),
  done = c(1, 1, 1, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3, 0, 0),
  after = c(NA, "Kick-off", "Research", "Design", "Prototype", "Design",
            "Build", "QA, User tests")
)
gantt_chart(plan, task = "task", start = "start", end = "end", group = "team",
            progress = "done", depends_on = "after",
            today = as.Date("2025-03-14"), title = "Product launch")
```

It also works as a simple timeline:

```{r}
reigns <- data.frame(
  monarch = c("Victoria", "Edward VII", "George V", "Edward VIII",
              "George VI", "Elizabeth II"),
  from = as.Date(c("1837-06-20", "1901-01-22", "1910-05-06", "1936-01-20",
                   "1936-12-11", "1952-02-06")),
  to = as.Date(c("1901-01-22", "1910-05-06", "1936-01-20", "1936-12-11",
                 "1952-02-06", "2022-09-08"))
)
gantt_chart(reigns, task = "monarch", start = "from", end = "to",
            colors = "#a463f2", date_format = "%Y")
```

## `candlestick_chart()` {#candlestick_chart}

A candlestick chart shows the open, high, low and close prices of each period: the body of a candle spans the open and the close (green when the price rose, red when it fell) and the wick spans the low and the high. Volumes are drawn below, and `moving_average` adds moving averages of the close. The periods are drawn side by side, so weekends leave no gaps. Move the mouse to read the prices of a period, scroll to zoom (the price axis fits the visible candles) and double-click to reset.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
days <- seq(as.Date("2025-01-01"), by = "day", length.out = 170)
days <- days[!format(days, "%u") %in% c("6", "7")][1:120]
close <- 100 * cumprod(1 + rnorm(120, 0.001, 0.018))
open <- c(100, head(close, -1)) * (1 + rnorm(120, 0, 0.004))
stock <- data.frame(
  day = days,
  open = open,
  high = pmax(open, close) * (1 + abs(rnorm(120, 0, 0.008))),
  low = pmin(open, close) * (1 - abs(rnorm(120, 0, 0.008))),
  close = close,
  volume = round(rlnorm(120, 13, 0.4))
)
candlestick_chart(stock, date = "day", open = "open", high = "high",
                  low = "low", close = "close", volume = "volume",
                  moving_average = c(10, 30), value_format = "$,.2f",
                  title = "A simulated stock")
```
